38.0.s.en: 1. Set your house in order, for you shall die:

38.0.0.en: 1 In those days was Hezekiah sick unto death. And Isaiah the prophet the son of Amoz came to him, and said unto him, “Thus saith the LORD, Set thine house in order: for thou shalt die, and not live.” 2 Then Hezekiah turned his face toward the wall, and prayed unto the LORD, 3 and said, “Remember now, O LORD, I beseech thee, how I have walked before thee in truth and with a perfect heart, and have done that which is good in thy sight.” And Hezekiah wept sore. 4 Then came the word of the LORD to Isaiah, saying, 5 “Go, and say to Hezekiah, Thus saith the LORD, the God of David thy father, I have heard thy prayer, I have seen thy tears: behold, I will add unto thy days fifteen years. 6 And I will deliver thee and this city out of the hand of the king of Assyria: and I will defend this city. 7 And this shall be a sign unto thee from the LORD, that the LORD will do this thing that he hath spoken; 8 Behold, I will bring again the shadow of the degrees, which is gone down in the sun dial of Ahaz, ten degrees backward.” So the sun returned ten degrees, by which degrees it was gone down.

38.0.1.en: “In those days was Hezekiah sick unto death” [1]. It is clear from this phrase and from verse [6] that Hezekiah’s illness came in the days of Sennacherib’s invasion. Some scholars think it was because of a plague that struck the city on account of the siege, while others think it was a psychological and physical collapse because of what had befallen his country.

38.0.2.en: Isaiah came to him, taking away from him every hope of remaining in this world, saying to him, “Set thine house in order: for thou shalt die, and not live” [1].

38.0.3.en: The news of his death was a shock to him, perhaps for one of the following reasons:

38.0.4.en: a. Like our teacher the Apostle Paul, he longed to depart, but he felt an obligation toward serving others.

38.0.5.en: b. Perhaps, like other men of the Old Testament who feared death, because in their minds it was bound up with sin and the wrath of God upon man.

38.1.0.en: c. Perhaps he expected to see in his days the Christ of the Lord, the Second Adam, the representative of all humanity, as is stated in his psalm [11].

38.1.1.en: d. Perhaps the main reason was that Manasseh had not yet been born (2 Kgs 21:1), so there was no one to succeed him on the throne. This troubled him, for how would the promise to the house of David be fulfilled, that it would remain forever? In this Hezekiah was very weak, unlike Abraham, who offered his son as a sacrifice without fear, trusting that God’s promise would surely be fulfilled, believing in God, who is able to raise him from the dead. Afterward Hezekiah begot “Manasseh,” a lover of idol worship, who provoked God’s wrath against Judah (2 Kgs 23:26).

38.1.2.en: In any case, Hezekiah was a man of prayer. The news did not rob him of his hope in the Lord; he knew how to pray and to wrestle. He turned his face toward the wall, perhaps facing the Temple as was the custom of the Jews, to pray to the Lord, saying, “Remember now, O LORD, I beseech thee, how I have walked before thee in truth and with a perfect (complete) heart, and have done that which is good in thy sight” [3]. Hezekiah looked upon his life as a journey in which he walked with God (Gen 5:24; 1 Kgs 9:4) with sincerity, not in absolute perfection but aiming toward perfection (Mt 5:45), with a single mind, neither hesitant nor deviating.

38.1.4.en: The divine command was issued to Isaiah to go to the king and tell him, “Thus saith the LORD, the God of David thy father, I have heard thy prayer, I have seen thy tears: behold, I will add unto thy days fifteen years” [5]. The answer came very quickly (2 Kgs 20:4); perhaps God spoke with Isaiah mouth to mouth before he left the royal palace, while he was giving spiritual counsel to the men of the palace to prepare the atmosphere for after the king’s death.

38.1.5.en: God heard Hezekiah’s prayer, looked upon his tears, and remembered His promise to David his father, since God remembers His covenant with the father in the case of his sons (Ex 20:5; Ps 89:28-29). He gave him the request of his heart, what he uttered with his tongue and what he spoke in his heart: He granted him length of days, deliverance from the king of Assyria, and protection for his city, or the capital of his kingdom, Jerusalem.

38.2.0.en: The Lord gave him a sign as he requested [22]; Hezekiah differed from his wicked father, who refused to ask a sign from God (Isa 7:10).

38.2.1.en: The divine sign came to confirm the fulfillment of the divine promise in this way: the sun returned ten degrees [8]. Some think it was merely a retreat of the shadow on the steps leading to a “balcony” in the palace or leading to the upper chamber. Others think it was an eclipse of the sun that occurred on January 11, 689 B.C. The sun is the true measure of time, and in God’s hand it is the mover of history, of events and of time itself. He used it as a sign in the days of Joshua (Josh 10:12), and also in the days of Hezekiah, and at the crucifixion of the Lord of glory, and before His final coming, when the sun shall be darkened...

38.2.2.en: God, the Father of lights, moves the sun and directs it for our edification.

38.2.3.en: Perhaps some will ask: Did God change His mind by lengthening Hezekiah’s life?

38.2.4.en: St. Augustine holds that Hezekiah ought to have died through natural causes such as illness, but that he added fifteen years to his life; this addition God knew before the foundation of the world, keeping it in His will. What He did by way of addition accomplished what was in God’s plan, since He knows what Hezekiah would do and what God would give him.

38.2.5.en: What should occupy our minds is not to inquire whether God had previously fixed Hezekiah’s age and then retracted it by adding fifteen years to it, but rather to realize the power of prayer in our lives, for it gave him life after he ought to have died according to the laws of nature. Prayer, as a clinging to God, the Giver of life, is able to do all things, and is victorious over death, the death of sin.

38.2.6.en: St. John Chrysostom says: [When we pray for the forgiveness of sins, we fulfill God’s will, and so we are assured that our prayer is answered.]

38.2.7.en: * Through prayer offerings were accepted; prayer is what turned the flood away from Noah; prayer healed barrenness and routed armies; prayer revealed mysteries; prayer divided the sea and made a way in the Jordan; prayer turned the sun back and stayed the moon, destroyed the defiled, and brought down fire.

38.2.8.en: Prayer shut the heaven, brought (men) out of the pit, rescued from the fire, and delivered from the sea. The power of prayer, like the power of pure fasting, is exceedingly great...

38.2.9.en: * Hezekiah prayed, and his prayer overcame 185,000 men, by means of an angel who acted as the commander of the army (2 Kgs 19:15, 35)...

38.2.10.en: * Daniel prayed, and his prayer stopped the mouths of the lions...

38.2.11.en: * Each one of our righteous fathers took up the weapon of prayer when sorrows met them, and they were delivered from them.

38.2.12.en: Father Aphrahat * Blessed is the man who agrees to be an intimate friend of faith and prayer, for he lives with a single mind...

38.2.13.en: * The prayer that rises in a man’s heart opens for us the door of heaven...

38.2.14.en: * Prayer establishes peace with the wrath of God...

38.2.15.en: St. Mar Ephrem the Syrian * Prayer is able to press upon Satan, who presses upon the human race. It is able to deliver from his hand and to free from every temptation in the world. For this reason our Lord rightly commanded us to watch and pray, lest we enter into temptation (Mt 26:41).

38.3.0.en: 9 The writing of Hezekiah king of Judah, when he had been sick, and was recovered of his sickness: 10 “I said in the cutting off of my days, I shall go to the gates of the grave: I am deprived of the residue of my years. 11 I said, I shall not see the LORD, even the LORD, in the land of the living: I shall behold man no more with the inhabitants of the world. 12 Mine age is departed, and is removed from me as a shepherd’s tent: I have cut off like a weaver my life: he will cut me off from the loom: from day even to night wilt thou make an end of me. 13 I cried until the morning; as a lion, so will he break all my bones: from day even to night wilt thou make an end of me. 14 Like a swallow chirping, so did I cry: I did mourn as a dove: mine eyes fail with looking upward: O LORD, I am oppressed; undertake for me. 15 What shall I say? he hath both spoken unto me, and himself hath done it: I shall go softly all my years in the bitterness of my soul. 16 O Lord, by these things men live, and in all these things is the life of my spirit: so wilt thou recover me, and make me to live. 17 Behold, for peace my bitterness was turned for me, and thou hast held my soul back from the pit of destruction: for thou hast cast all my sins behind thy back. 18 For the grave cannot praise thee, death cannot celebrate thee: they that go down into the pit cannot hope for thy truth. 19 The living, the living, he shall praise thee, as I do this day: the father to the children shall make known thy truth. 20 The LORD is for my salvation: therefore we will play on our stringed instruments all the days of our life in the house of the LORD.”

38.3.1.en: a. We often remember God in time of distress and hardship but forget Him in time of relief and joy. Hezekiah, however, showed himself a man of prayer and tears in the midst of suffering, and a man of praise at the time of relief, who knew how to thank God for His benefits.

38.3.2.en: In this psalm he showed himself to be a man of prayer, a man of praise, a poet and psalmist, a stranger in the world, full of hope in the Lord who saves from death and gives joyful life.

38.3.3.en: b. It was good that Hezekiah offered this psalm as a sacrifice of thanksgiving to God, the Giver of life, and it would have been better for him to offer his very life as a sacrifice of thanksgiving to Him; but sadly he offered a song of thanksgiving without a life of thanksgiving, for it is said: “But Hezekiah rendered not again according to the benefit done unto him; for his heart was lifted up: therefore there was wrath upon him, and upon Judah and Jerusalem” (2 Chr 32:25).

38.3.4.en: It befits us to praise God not only with our tongues, uttering psalms of thanksgiving to Him, but also with all the members of our body, our feelings and our senses, as well as our practical conduct, so that our whole life is turned into a harp of varied strings playing a symphony of love to God, our Creator and Savior.

38.4.0.en: c. Hezekiah’s psalm shows how he suffered at the beginning from a spirit of despair, for he said: “I said in the cutting off of my days, I shall go to the gates of the grave: I am deprived of the residue of my years” [10]. Hezekiah was about thirty-nine years old; he felt that in the prime of his youth his happy days had been cut off and that he was deprived of serving God and His people, which he had set in his heart to complete throughout the years of his life. It is as if he were repeating the words of King David: “For I said in my haste, I am cut off from before thine eyes” (Ps 31:22).

38.5.0.en: d. Perhaps Hezekiah expected to see the Christ of the Lord in his days, or hoped for His coming incarnate from his seed, and here he was dying without offspring. Therefore he cried out in despair: “I said, I shall not see the LORD, even the LORD, in the land of the living: I shall behold man no more with the inhabitants of the world” [11]. Thus he was awaiting to see the Christ of the Lord here, or to enjoy the glory of the Lord in the other life, but despair shattered him.

38.5.1.en: “I said, I shall not see the LORD”... What hope have we in this world or in the world to come unless we enjoy the sight of the Lord, here through the eyes of the heart by faith, and there face to face!

38.5.2.en: * Blessed, thrice blessed, indeed many times blessed are those who are counted worthy to behold that glory. Of this the prophet says: “Let the wicked be taken away, that he behold not the glory of the LORD” [(Isa 36:10) LXX]. May God grant that none of us be taken away or excluded from beholding (the Lord)... For why do we live? Why do we breathe? What will become of us if we fail to behold our Lord and are not granted this? If those who cannot behold the light of the sun count life harsher than death, what will be the state of those who are deprived of that Light?

38.5.3.en: St. John Chrysostom * Before I show you our God, show me your man; and give me proof that the eyes of your soul can see and the ears of your heart can hear. On the contrary, those whose eyes are afflicted with the cloud of sin cannot behold God...

38.5.4.en: When you are removed from your corruptible nature and put on incorruption, you will see God, since you will be made worthy of it. For God will give life to your body and make it, with your immortal soul, deathless; then you will see the One who alone is immortal, if you believe in Him now.

38.5.5.en: St. Theophilus of Antioch e. He presents several similes by which he expresses his temporal life:

38.6.0.en: The first simile: the shepherd’s tent, quickly moved [12]. This creates the sense of being a stranger; we have no place in the world in which to settle, so that we are like our father Abraham, who did not cease to walk on the journey of his life... We remain in this moving tent until we pass over to an eternal dwelling not made with human hands. Our teacher the Apostle Paul used this simile (2 Cor 5:1), and also St. Peter (2 Pet 1:14).

38.6.1.en: The second simile: weaving, “I have cut off like a weaver my life: he will cut me off from the loom: from day even to night wilt thou make an end of me” [12]. Thus God weaves our life like a garment cut from the loom, woven according to the size of each one’s body; it does not last long but only for a while, like one who wears it for a single day and night and then it is taken off. As Eliphaz the Temanite says: “They are destroyed from morning to evening” (Job 4:19-20).

38.7.0.en: The third simile: the prey whose bones the lion breaks, all of them, between one day and night [13].

38.8.0.en: The fourth simile: like a swallow chirping, he cries out in weakness, for his voice grew faint because of illness, or rather because of his despair of recovery; his voice became like the moaning of a dove [14], and his eyes became unable to look upward [14].

38.9.0.en: f. We find a swift transition from the feeling of the bitterness of the despairing soul [15] to the experience of new life, for he says without preface: “O Lord, by these things men live, and in all these things is the life of my spirit: so wilt thou recover me, and make me to live” [16]... He passes from death to life and from bitterness to peace [17]; the secret of this is the intervention of the Lord Christ, and the discovery of His divine work of salvation, for he says: “For thou hast cast all my sins behind thy back... The LORD is for my salvation: therefore we will play on our stringed instruments all the days of our life in the house of the LORD” [17, 20].

38.9.1.en: What did he find in his Savior?

38.10.0.en: First: his life was changed from an exceedingly terrifying journey, bitter to the soul, into a calm life filled with peace, in which the believer fears not even the pit [17].

38.10.1.en: Second: his soul rejoices not because of his healing from the illness and the length of his life, but because of the forgiveness of all his sins [17].

38.11.0.en: Third: he came to long to hand on to the coming generations this new life, or the truth of God [19].

38.12.0.en: Fourth: all the rest of his life was turned into a psalm of unceasing joy [20], which he sings as in the house of the Lord. For this reason St. Athanasius the Apostolic speaks to us of the feast (or joy) as being “Christ” Himself, the secret of our constant gladness. As he said: [Only those who live in Christ are able to glorify God and bless Him; by this they go up to the feast.]

38.12.1.en: In any case, the believer who lives in Christ enjoys a life of constant joy and also constant thanksgiving, in the midst of his sufferings and his joys.

38.12.2.en: * There is no time more fitting for a man to hold feelings of thanksgiving toward God than when he is in trials and troubles. And there is no better time for offering thanks than when he comes to rest after struggles and trials.

38.12.3.en: St. Athanasius the Apostolic * Prayer is a joy that expresses itself in thanksgiving.

38.12.4.en: Father Evagrius * Through spiritual prayer and utterances of thanksgiving we rise from the earth to the heights.

38.13.s.en: 3. His healing by a lump of figs:

38.13.0.en: 21 For Isaiah had said, “Let them take a lump of figs, and lay it for a plaister upon the boil, and he shall recover.” 22 Hezekiah also had said, “What is the sign that I shall go up to the house of the LORD?”

38.13.1.en: Isaiah the prophet asked Hezekiah to place a lump of figs [a cake of pressed figs] on the inflamed part of his body so that he would be healed... Why? So that God might declare that although He is the Physician who heals, He uses the medicines and material means that He created to meet our needs; and at that time they used to place a lump of pressed figs on inflamed places of the body as a treatment. On the other hand, healing is a free divine gift that God gives of His own accord.

38.14.0.en: The lump of figs, like the cluster of grapes, both point to the living life of the Church. For the fig holds countless very fine seeds; a single seed has no value or taste unless it is joined with the rest of the seeds under one covering that gathers them together, as if in the sweetness of love and unity. This is the secret of the Church’s sweetness. And this is the cause of our healing: with the personal, hidden relationship each of us has with God, we gather together like a sweet fig in the mouth of God. Therefore Hezekiah said of the sign of his healing, “that I shall go up to the house of the LORD” [22], to gather with the people of God through the Lord Himself.
